translationStringList.COLOUR_SET_EXPLANATION:
Which colours shall be used in the user interface, for example when assigning a colour to a private tag. The 4 colour sets represent selections according to colour blindness accessibility.

22: These colours are carefully selected to be tasteful and independently easily distinguishable. This full set is usable by approximately 95 % of the general population which has normal colour vision.

18: About 4 % of the population have all three types of cones (RGB), but the red or green cones may not be fully functional, making it more difficult to distinguish green/yellow and blue/purple combinations. Colours that get too close to each other, such as olive, which becomes like brown, are removed.

9: A further 1 % of the population are missing red or green cones. Roughly speaking, they see colours with wavelengths longer than cyan (e.g. red, green) as shades of yellow, and colours with wavelengths shorter than cyan (e.g. purple) as shades of blue. Since they appear to have the same hue, the only differentiating factors become luminance and chromaticity. Orange and yellow can still be distinguished, but orange looks like a darker yellow.

5: The final 0.01 % of the population may have weak or missing blue cones, only one type of cone, or no cones at all. People with tritanomaly (weak blue cones) can see almost the entire spectrum just fine, while people with tritanopia (no blue cones) see, roughly, yellow through purple as cyan, and magenta through orange as red. This set also caters to people who cannot distinguish any hues. Yellow becomes light grey, and blue becomes dark grey.

Source: Sasha Trubetskoy
